channel.title: Oddly Wired
channel.description: One checked psychology fact a day. Every claim names the study behind it.

item.title: You are a slave to your previous assumptions.
item.description: Schema-based processing leads to faster information integration at the cost of detail.

item.title: You make judgements based on how quickly you think.
item.description: The feeling of ease, or processing fluency, acts as a heuristic for validity.

item.title: You focus on what you expect to see.
item.description: Feature integration theory suggests we use focused attention at a specific location to bind pre-attentively registered features into a coherent object.

item.title: You remember stories better than sequences of abstract facts.
item.description: The dual-coding theory suggests that memory is enhanced by pairing verbal and visual information.

item.title: You are smarter when you slow down deliberately.
item.description: The Cognitive Reflection Test predicts performance on logical tasks by measuring impulse inhibition.

item.title: Your mind maps out space even in the dark.
item.description: Mental maps are formed using dead reckoning rather than just landmarks.

item.title: Your motivation drops when you feel external pressure.
item.description: Autonomy is a fundamental requirement for long-term intrinsic task engagement.

item.title: Your physical movements can prime your mental speed.
item.description: Mental rotation of objects takes longer when the angle of rotation is greater.

item.title: You can be deaf even when your ears work.
item.description: In inattentional deafness, you fail to notice obvious sounds when focused on a visual task.

item.title: You process known words faster than scrambled letters.
item.description: The priming effect allows you to identify a word significantly faster after seeing a related concept.

item.title: You have a bottleneck in your visual attention.
item.description: When two distinct targets appear in rapid succession, you frequently miss the second one.

item.title: Your brain can treat a fake hand as real.
item.description: In the rubber hand illusion, touch on a hidden hand causes a sensation in a visible fake hand.

item.title: You repeat a lie until it sounds like truth.
item.description: The illusory truth effect shows that repeated statements are judged as more likely to be true than non-repeated statements, even when the information contradicts existing knowledge.

item.title: You lose time with every shift in focus.
item.description: A 2001 study found that task-switching costs result in significant drops in efficiency when moving between different types of mental work.

item.title: Your brain registers social rejection as physical pain.
item.description: A 2003 study found that the same neural regions that process physical pain light up when you experience social exclusion.

item.title: You want things that you do not enjoy.
item.description: Incentive salience distinguishes between the act of wanting a reward and the actual pleasure of consuming it.

item.title: You believe objects have a hidden true nature.
item.description: Psychological essentialism asserts that people believe certain categories—primarily natural kinds—possess an underlying, unobservable essence that determines their identity.

item.title: You twist evidence to support a chosen path.
item.description: The study titled 'Biased interpretation of evidence' by Carlson and Russo, which demonstrates how people distort new information to favor a preferred option, was published in 2001.

item.title: You make more rational decisions in a foreign language.
item.description: A 2012 study found that people are significantly less biased when making decisions in a second language.

item.title: You are more likely to lie when you feel anonymous.
item.description: A 2010 study found that people in a darkened room were more likely to cheat on a math test than those in a well-lit one.

item.title: You perceive time differently depending on what you see.
item.description: A 2011 study found that viewing 'high-arousal' images causes you to overestimate the duration of time that has passed.

item.title: You make more ethical decisions in the morning.
item.description: A 2014 study found that people are more likely to behave dishonestly as the day progresses.

item.title: The scent of your environment dictates your ability to focus.
item.description: A 2003 study found that exposure to peppermint odor significantly improves performance on tasks requiring sustained attention.

item.title: You fear losing money more than gaining it.
item.description: Loss aversion is the tendency to prefer avoiding losses over acquiring equivalent gains, with a median loss aversion coefficient of approximately 2.25.

item.title: Your confidence in a decision comes after the act.
item.description: Post-decision dissonance reduction causes people to retroactively inflate the value of a choice they just made.

item.title: Your brain prioritizes unfinished tasks to force closure.
item.description: The Zeigarnik effect dictates that interrupted tasks are remembered significantly better than completed ones.

item.title: Sleeping on it improves your problem-solving abilities.
item.description: A 2004 study found that participants who slept were significantly more likely to gain insight into a hidden mathematical rule than those who remained awake.

item.title: Your name influences your career choices.
item.description: Research in the early 2000s suggested a correlation between initials and career choice, but this has been largely debunked as an artifact of confounders.

item.title: Music tempo changes how you shop.
item.description: A 1986 study found that stores playing slower music saw significantly higher sales than those playing faster tempos.

item.title: Ambient noise levels determine your creativity.
item.description: A 2012 study found that moderate levels of ambient noise boost abstract thinking compared to total silence.

item.title: Standing tall makes you believe your own thoughts more.
item.description: A 2009 study found that participants who maintained an upright posture reported more confidence in their own written thoughts.

item.title: Expressing gratitude consistently rewires your daily outlook.
item.description: A 2003 study showed that writing about things you are grateful for increases well-being compared to focusing on daily hassles.

item.title: A fake smile can change your mood.
item.description: A 1988 study claimed that participants rated cartoons as funnier when holding a pen in their teeth, but these findings have not been replicated in subsequent large-scale research.

item.title: Red colors subtly kill your performance on tests.
item.description: A 2007 study by Elliot et al. in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: General found that viewing the color red before an exam can result in statistically significant performance decrements, but these are small in magnitude, not a 20% reduction.

item.title: Holding a warm drink makes you perceive others as kinder.
item.description: In a 2008 study by Williams and Bargh, participants holding a warm coffee cup judged a stranger as having a warmer personality than those holding iced coffee, though subsequent attempts to replicate these findings have failed.

item.title: You forget your intentions when you walk through doorways.
item.description: A 2011 study found that entering a new room significantly decreases your ability to recall information from the previous one.

item.title: You are driven either by hope or caution.
item.description: Regulatory focus theory identifies two different motivational systems: a promotion focus on achievement and a prevention focus on safety.

item.title: You fail because you trust your first instinct.
item.description: The Cognitive Reflection Test shows that people often fail simple logic puzzles by relying on intuitive, incorrect answers.

item.title: Your judgment is relative to what came before.
item.description: The sequential contrast effect shows that your evaluation of an object changes based on the quality of the item immediately preceding it.

item.title: You only act when the result seems possible.
item.description: Expectancy theory states that motivation is the multiplicative product of three factors: expectancy (that effort leads to performance), instrumentality (that performance leads to a reward), and valence (the value the individual places on that reward).

item.title: You cannot ignore the meaning of a word.
item.description: The Stroop effect demonstrates that you are slower at identifying the ink color of a word that names a different color.

item.title: You feel worse when your friend succeeds.
item.description: Self-evaluation maintenance theory explains why your self-esteem drops when a close friend performs exceptionally well.

item.title: You prefer a smaller reward that is certain.
item.description: Research shows people systematically choose lower-value, certain rewards over higher-value options involving uncertainty.

item.title: Warm coffee makes you judge people more kindly.
item.description: A 2008 study reported this finding, but the effect has not been successfully replicated in later research.

item.title: You are more likely to trust a stranger if they share your birthday.
item.description: Implicit egotism is a controversial hypothesis proposing a subconscious preference for self-associated stimuli, but it has not been conclusively proven or reliably replicated.

item.title: You mistake the ease of recalling a reason for the validity of that reason.
item.description: The availability heuristic leads you to treat information that is easier to remember as more important or frequent.

item.title: Your brain prefers to categorize people by race to process information faster.
item.description: People are generally more accurate at recognizing faces of their own race, a phenomenon known as the cross-race effect or own-race bias.

item.title: You believe your thoughts are more transparent to others than they really are.
item.description: The illusion of transparency leads you to overestimate how well others can read your emotional state.

item.title: A moment of awe makes you feel like time is slowing down.
item.description: Experiencing awe expands your perception of time, leaving you feeling like you have more of it.

item.title: You assume a name is famous simply because you saw it earlier.
item.description: The false fame effect leads people to misattribute familiarity to celebrity status.
